1.pericope_label: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me: the cry unanswered and the fathers who trusted

schools.summary: Augustine gives the words to the crucified sustaining the person of the old man nailed to the cross with him, which accounts for a cry that speaks of sins and does not know the reason for its own forsaking.

Calvin dismisses the search for a mystery in the title as needless perplexity over a small matter; Gill guards the desertion with distinctions, denying that the union was dissolved or the love withdrawn and allowing only the loss of the sense of joy, and makes the divine holiness a reason quieting the sufferer.

Henry reports both a christological and a musical reading of the title; Spurgeon attends to the manner of the cry, finding faith in the doubled address and strength in the divine name used, so that the appeal is made in grief but not in doubt.

Clarke canvasses the guesses at the title and proposes that eastern poems often bear names unrelated to their subject, citing examples from his own manuscripts, and conjectures that the psalm was written where the father of the tribes had wrestled; Wesley divides the fulfilment between David and Christ.

Ellicott refuses an individual sufferer, preferring pious Israel in trouble, and reworks the wording at several points including a conjecture that completes the parallelism, reading the praises of Israel as themselves the throne of God; Keil and Delitzsch keep David under the persecution by Saul and record the rival datings.

debates: Who is the sufferer of this psalm? Keil and Delitzsch keep David under the persecution by Saul while recording that one critic dates the psalm before the destruction of the city and another in the exile, and that a third confesses the question insoluble; Ellicott holds that the tone suits the whole of pious Israel better than any individual; Augustine gives the words to the crucified speaking in the person of the old man; Gill and Spurgeon read them of Christ throughout; Wesley divides the fulfilment between David and a greater sufferer.

What does the title mean? Henry reports a christological reading of the hind of the morning alongside the view that it names only a tune; Clarke reviews instrument, tune and band, prefers the suggestion that it names the psalm itself on the analogy of eastern books whose titles bear no relation to their contents, and gives examples; Calvin dismisses the whole search as needless perplexity over a matter of small importance.
outliers: Clarke supports his reading of the title from manuscripts in his own collection, naming eastern works called the Country of Roses, which mentions no roses, the Gallery of Pictures, which contains no picture.

Ellicott reads the praises of Israel as forming the throne itself, so that the ever-ascending praise of the people takes the place of the outstretched wings of the cherubim, and prefers this to the rabbinical rendering.
themes: a cry that keeps its hold while asking why
desertion felt but not deserved
the holiness of God as answer and as comfort
praise as the throne of God
the trust of the fathers as precedent

6.pericope_label: But I am a worm, and no man: the mockery of the bystanders and the appeal to infancy

schools.summary: Henry argues that many particulars here were never true of David and must belong to a greater sufferer treading the winepress alone; Spurgeon counts the two reasons of the petition as a double knock at mercy gate and dwells on the crushing weight of absolute friendlessness.

Gill grounds the name worm in the opinion men held of the sufferer rather than in his origin or nature, expounds the taunt as reported speech, and uses the appeal to infancy against the claim that the manner of the birth was miraculous as well as the conception.

Clarke denies that our Lord could have used the word worm of himself, then quotes an old Psalter that reads it of the virgin birth, and holds the mockery primarily true of the insults David suffered, the evangelist describing the later conduct in the earlier language; Wesley says the verse suits Christ better than David.

Ellicott reads the worm as extreme degradation, notes that the Greek verb here recurs in the gospel account, and raises the choice between a reported taunt and an imperative that tells the sufferer to roll himself on God; Keil and Delitzsch weigh the double sense of the verb in the following verse.

debates: Can the sufferer call himself a worm? Clarke says he can see no sense in which our Lord could use the terms, though David might use them of his own vileness, and Wesley and Henry answer that the verse and its neighbours fit Christ better than David, Henry adding that many particulars were never true of David at all; Gill resolves it by making the name express the opinion of others rather than the nature of the speaker, and Ellicott takes it simply for degradation and helplessness.

Is the mockers second sentence a report or a command? Ellicott notes that the old Greek, the evangelist and one modern scholar read it as a report, he trusted on the Lord, while the form is generally taken as an imperative putting into the mockers mouths the words roll thyself on God; Gill expounds only the reported taunt, observing that the jeer was aimed at the trust rather than at its object.
outliers: Clarke old Psalter reads a worm and no man as a statement of the incarnation, born of the maiden without man seed and not man only but God also, and lists the spitting, the buffeting, the piercing with thorns and the choosing of the thief.

Gill turns the appeal to infancy into an argument against a miraculous manner of birth, granting the miracle of the conception but insisting that the term was the usual nine months and the birth like that of other infants.
themes: degradation expressed as a worm
mockery aimed at trust itself
a taunt that may be a command
God claimed from the womb onward
the crushing weight of friendlessness

12.pericope_label: Many bulls have compassed me: the beasts, the dissolution of the body, and the pierced hands and feet

schools.summary: Gill assigns the bulls and dogs to the rulers and the soldiers, refers the pouring out like water to the sweat in the garden or to the tears or the blood, and reports the ancient renderings that make the bones numbered by others.

Clarke explains the beasts from natural history and local geography, denies that the dissolution of the body can be spoken of Christ in any sound theologic sense, and yet decides the great textual crux for the piercing and treats that verse and the parting of the garments as direct revelation; Wesley holds that neither clause can be applied to David.

Ellicott locates the point of the animal figures in pampered insolence and pack hunting, prefers emaciation to dislocation in the bones, doubts that the disputed root can mean to pierce and renders a binding of the limbs that cuts them, and holds that the gospel use of the parted garments adds a refinement not in the psalm; Keil and Delitzsch read the dissolution as the physiology of crucifixion.

debates: What stands in the text where the hands and feet are named? Clarke sets out the manuscripts, the polyglots and the ancient versions, observes that the whole difference lies between two easily confused letters, decides for they pierced, and treats the verse as a direct revelation since the psalmist own hands were never pierced; Ellicott calls the word a battle-ground, agrees that as a lion yields no sense and that the pointing must be given up, but doubts whether the root can mean to pierce at all and renders instead a binding of the hands and feet so tight that it cuts them.

How far may the sufferings here be read of Christ? Clarke denies that the dissolution of the body can be spoken of him in any sound theologic sense, whether in the garden or on the cross, and then within three verses calls the piercing and the parted garments direct revelation sealed with eternal truth; Keil and Delitzsch read the very verse he refuses as the physiology of crucifixion; Ellicott holds that the gospel application of the parted garments adds a refinement not present in the psalm; Gill and Wesley read the whole passage of Christ.
outliers: Ellicott renders the disputed clause as a band of villains surrounding the sufferer and binding his hands and feet so as to cut them, rejecting the sense pierce as too doubtful to rest on.
Clarke quotes his old Psalter again for the pouring out like water, in the version that they reckoned no more of slaying him than of spilling water.
themes: enemies figured as beasts in packs
a body already dissolving
a text that turns on one letter
garments divided by lot
suffering described before it happened

19.pericope_label: But be not thou far from me: deliverance sought from the sword, the dog, the lion and the horns

schools.summary: Gill reads the lion either of the adversary overcome in the garden and on the cross or of the most powerful human enemies.

Clarke makes the psalm the humanity of Christ speaking to his divinity and assigns every expression of weakness to the human nature, takes the darling as the only one ever born without the agency of man, and expounds the last beast by natural history and by his old Psalter; Wesley reads the darling as a soul left destitute and the closing clause as an answer already given.

Ellicott derives the darling from its usage of an only child and of a desolate person, identifies the last beast as a buffalo or antelope, and weighs three constructions of the closing clause, preferring the one that preserves the parallelism; Keil and Delitzsch take the sword as an example of the enemy weapon and the hand of the dog as its paw.

debates: What is the darling that is to be delivered? Clarke renders it my only one and applies it to the sufferer as the only human being ever produced without the agency of man; Wesley applies it to his soul, so called because left alone and destitute of friends and helpers; Ellicott keeps to usage, where the word serves for an only child and for a person left desolate and stands here as a synonym for soul or life.

How does the closing clause run? Ellicott offers three constructions, that God hear him calling from among the horns, that the prayer break off into exultant faith with thou hast heard me, or that with the old versions he be saved poor and humble as he is, and prefers the first for the parallelism; Wesley takes it flatly as an answer already given.
outliers: Clarke states that the humanity of Christ here speaks to his divinity, and that the man could not have worked the miracles while the God in that man could not have suffered the sufferings, yet one person appears to do and to suffer all.

Clarke expounds the unicorn from natural history, proposing the rhinoceros among land animals and the narwhal among sea creatures, and citing a horn in his own museum which measures seven feet four inches.
themes: petition renewed at the extremity
weakness assigned to the human nature
a life left solitary
beasts standing for enemies
a prayer turning into an answer

22.pericope_label: I will declare thy name unto my brethren: the vow of praise and the meal of the afflicted

schools.summary: Henry marks that the same speaker who began complaining ends triumphing and that the epistle applies the first words of the triumph as it does those of the complaint; Spurgeon describes the change as a tempest turning to calm and proposes that the passage is a soliloquy uttered in the mind in the last moments before death.

Gill takes the brethren for the apostles and all believers rather than kinsmen, rejects the reading that limits the fearers of the Lord to Gentile proselytes, and reads the eating wholly of spiritual food.

Clarke reads the summons as addressed to the Jews while allowing that the fearers may be Gentile proselytes, distinguishes the smaller assembly of the earlier verse from the great assembly here and assigns them to Jews and Gentiles, and keeps the sacrificial logic of the meal; Wesley makes the great congregation the universal church of both and reads the eating of spiritual blessings.

Ellicott prefers the afflicted to the meek, argues that the word points to the Levites and that the banquet figure comes from the feast after a sacrifice; Keil and Delitzsch call the passage the evangel itself, correct the ancient versions on the word for affliction, refuse to spiritualise the vows, and note how far the results transcend David own experience.

debates: Who are those summoned to praise? Gill reports that some Jewish interpreters restrict those who fear the Lord to Gentile proselytes, set over against the seed of Jacob named beside them, and rejects the restriction in favour of all the people of God; Clarke takes the summons as addressed to the Jews to profit by the gospel while thinking the fearers may indeed be Gentiles and proselytes, since the seed of Jacob and of Israel are named separately; Keil and Delitzsch address it to Israel so far as it fears the God of revelation.

Who eats at the promised meal, and what is eaten? Ellicott prefers the afflicted to the meek, holds that the word points to the Levites, and derives the figure from the feast that followed a great sacrifice; Clarke keeps the sacrificial logic, that those who offered fed on what they offered; Gill and Wesley read the eating wholly of spiritual food and spiritual blessings; Keil and Delitzsch observe that the whole prospect transcends anything in the historical experience of David.
outliers: Spurgeon proposes that these verses be read as part of a soliloquy uttered in the mind of the sufferer during the last few moments before his death, rather than as words spoken aloud.

Keil and Delitzsch refuse to spiritualise the paying of vows, insisting that it need not be taken as purely ethical rather than ritual, since the rescued man will bring the thank-offerings he vowed in the extremest peril.
themes: complaint turning into thanksgiving
a sufferer naming his hearers brethren
praise summoned from a whole people
vows paid in kind
a meal for the afflicted

27.pericope_label: All the ends of the world shall remember: the nations turned, the seed that serves, and the work declared

schools.summary: Gill confines the promise to the elect among the Gentiles, takes the fat of the earth for the rich and the rulers while reporting a Jewish inversion of the clause, and answers the old versions and the paraphrase on the seed by making it chiefly Gentile.

Clarke extends the promise from nations to families, emends the hardest verse on the authority of the ancient versions and his old Psalter so that it becomes the psalmist own vow, and expects the great and kings to embrace the gospel; Wesley calls the passage an evident prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles and makes the last verse the key to the whole psalm.

Ellicott judges the fat ones out of place in the verse and offers two emendations to restore the parallelism, reading the closing words of a man too poor to keep body and soul together, and renders the seed as posterity told of in the coming generation; Keil and Delitzsch explain the remembering of the heathen from a knowledge already among them and call the eating a meal that satisfies the soul.

debates: What does the text say where none can keep alive his own soul? Clarke reports that the Latin, Syriac, Greek, Ethiopic, Arabic and old English versions read instead that my soul shall live to him and my seed shall serve him, believes this the true reading, and takes it as the psalmist own vow; Ellicott alters the same verse on different grounds, holding that the fat ones of the earth are out of place among the eaters and injure the parallelism, and rendering the last clause of a man too poor to keep body and soul together rather than of one already dead; Gill and Wesley expound the received text.

Who are the fat upon earth? Gill takes them for the rich and the rulers, reports a Jewish reading that inverts the clause so that the meek eat the fat of the earth, and notes that the word carries the sense of ashes, so that the great are themselves dust and ashes; Clarke expects kings and the great to embrace the gospel; Wesley has them feeding on the bread of life; Ellicott holds that they do not belong in the verse at all.
outliers: Clarke turns the disputed verse into a personal vow of the psalmist, that he will live to this Saviour while he lives and that his spiritual posterity will serve him through all generations, and states the three small changes of letter the reading requires.

Wesley makes the closing verse the key to the whole psalm, teaching that the writer speaks not of himself but of things to be done in after ages, and that what is declared is the work of God and not of man.
themes: the nations remembering what they had forgotten
a gospel reaching families as well as peoples
a verse recovered by conjecture
the rich and the dying at one table
a work declared to generations unborn
